title: Movie-watching outperforms rest for functional connectivity-based prediction of behavior.

items.referenceFact: Tested hypothesis that movie-watching connectivity improves prediction of trait-like phenotypes compared to rest.
items.generatedFact: Tested the hypothesis that functional connectivity during movie viewing yields more accurate predictions of cognitive and emotional trait scores than rest.

quotes: Furthermore, there has been relatively less work on how brain state affects connectivity-based predictions of traits outside the cognitive domain—for example, emotion and affect. Naturalistic tasks also raise the intriguing possibility of tailoring stimulus content to the construct to be predicted—for example, using a stimulus that evokes feelings of suspense or unease to predict anxiety, or one that evokes feelings of suspicion to predict paranoia ( Finn et al., 2018 ). Here, we test the hypothesis that data collected during movie watching improves functional connectivity-based behavior prediction compared to data collected at rest.

quotes: Whether this benefit extends to naturalistic paradigms, and to non-cognitive domains such as emotional traits, had not been directly tested. The present study tested the hypothesis that functional connectivity recorded during movie viewing yields more accurate predictions of cognitive and emotional trait scores than connectivity measured during rest. Secondary aims included determining the minimum data duration needed for accurate prediction, examining which stimulus features associate with greater predictive accuracy, and evaluating whether any gain could be attributed to differences in arousal between conditions. --- ## 2.

quotes: Movie-watching outperforms rest for prediction of behavior traits Our main goal was to compare how well cognition and emotion scores could be predicted based on functional brain connectivity during rest or movie watching. REST runs were 900 TRs, or 15:00, in duration, while MOVIE runs ranged from 769 to 800 TRs (12:49–13:20) following removal of rest periods between clips (see Methods ). For each subject for each run, we created a whole-brain functional connectivity matrix by calculating the Pearson correlation of activity timecourses between each pair of nodes in a predefined 268-node atlas ( Shen et al., 2013 ).

quotes: Connectome-based predictive modeling with leave-one-family-out cross-validation demonstrated that movie-watching connectivity consistently outperformed rest: median Spearman correlations for cognition reached 0.41 for the most predictive movie run, compared with 0.26 for the corresponding rest run, and one movie run yielded significant prediction of emotion score (rs = 0.18) whereas no rest run did. The advantage persisted with as little as approximately 2.5 minutes of data from single video clips. Eye-tracking analyses indicated that differences in arousal could not account for the advantage.

quotes: Results We used fMRI and behavioral data from 176 healthy subjects made available as part of the Human Connectome Project 7T dataset ( Van Essen et al., 2013 ). Functional runs of interest included two resting-state runs and four movie-watching runs, each approximately 15 min in duration. While data were acquired in four separate sessions, we focused on the two sessions that contained movie-watching runs (first and fourth). For each subject, REST1, MOVIE1 and MOVIE2 were acquired together in that order in a single session (referred to here as “Session 1″), and REST4, MOVIE3 and MOVIE4 were acquired in that order in a separate session (“Session 2″) on the following day or two days later.

quotes: Functional runs used a gradient-echo EPI sequence: TR = 1000 ms, TE = 22.2 ms, flip angle = 45°, 1.6 mm isotropic voxels, 85 slices, multiband factor 5. Two resting-state runs (REST1, REST4; each 900 TRs / 15:00 min) and four movie-watching runs (MOVIE1–4; between 901 and 921 TRs before clip-parsing) were analyzed. During rest, participants fixated on a central crosshair. During movie runs, participants passively viewed 4–5 audiovisual clips drawn from independent and Hollywood films (individual clip duration range: 1:03–4:19 min:sec), separated by 20-second rest blocks.

This 10-fold cross-validation was repeated 100 times with distinct fold splits. Accuracy was quantified as the Spearman rank correlation between predicted and observed scores.
